domain_assessment.domain: Municipal building and fire-code plan review involving a performance-based atrium smoke-control design
domain_assessment.role: Plan-review official in a building and fire division responsible for permitting and life-safety sign-off
domain_assessment.objective: Complete a legally timely and technically defensible review of an adaptive-reuse high-rise while protecting occupant safety in a fire event
domain_assessment.incident_type: A minor trash-chute fire that was controlled by sprinklers but prompted post-incident scrutiny of the atrium smoke-control model and system assumptions

decision_points.summary: Approve the performance-based CFD smoke-control design for the atrium without requiring external peer review.
evidence_before: The atrium geometry did not fit prescriptive smoke-control provisions.
The engineering firm had extensive performance-based atrium-design experience.
A neighboring jurisdiction had approved a similar design from the same firm.
The participant had the CFD report and documentation package.
The department had no budget for outside peer review.
A 30-day statutory review deadline and staffing shortfall applied.
evidence_after: Fire-door deficiencies were found during construction.
The developer later requested early occupancy.
A trash-chute fire later prompted review of atrium smoke behavior.
goals_constraints: Achieve safe fire and life-safety sign-off.
Work within limited staffing and peer-review resources.
Respond to city pressure to maintain housing-project momentum.
alternatives: Approve based on the submitted CFD report and documentation package.
Require an external peer review of CFD assumptions.
Apply deeper independent internal scrutiny to key CFD inputs before approval.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant reports relying heavily on the firm's reputation and neighboring-jurisdiction approval, with reduced independent scrutiny of the CFD input assumptions.
decision_points.time_pressure: High because of the statutory 30-day clock, staffing shortage, lack of outside-review budget, and broader pressure to keep housing projects moving.
decision_points.uncertainty: Objectively material because the design was non-prescriptive and unpeer-reviewed; subjectively lower than warranted because the participant trusted the firm's reputation.

decision_points.summary: Select the established prescriptive commissioning protocol rather than the better-matched risk-informed protocol.
evidence_before: Option A was described in guidance as better matched to the atrium's geometry.
Option A had partly qualitative pass/fail thresholds.
Option B had clear binary pass/fail criteria.
Option B was easier to defend administratively.
Option B was known to be less sensitive to some relevant atrium failure modes.
evidence_after: Temporary occupancy was requested before full integration testing.
goals_constraints: Use criteria that can be defended consistently.
Avoid an administratively difficult qualitative judgment.
alternatives: Use the newer risk-informed protocol better suited to actual atrium geometry.
Use the older prescriptive smoke test with binary criteria.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant selected Option B because its thresholds were clear and defensible, despite recognizing that Option A was likely the better technical fit.
decision_points.time_pressure: No acute decision-specific deadline is stated, although the broader project schedule remained relevant.
decision_points.uncertainty: Explicit and central: Option A required judgment under qualitative thresholds, whereas Option B offered a clean binary decision rule.

decision_points.summary: Concentrate follow-up inspection on three floors after fire-door deficiencies were observed on those floors.
evidence_before: Deficiencies were identified on floors 8, 11, and 14.
Approximately 150 doors had been inspected at that time.
The contractor crews rotated randomly across the building.
Three deficiencies were described as compatible with ordinary project-level variation.
evidence_after: The participant redirected follow-up inspections to floors 8, 11, and 14.
The participant later acknowledged that the apparent pattern felt more certain than the evidence warranted.
goals_constraints: Identify whether fire-door defects were isolated or systemic.
alternatives: Concentrate on the three flagged floors.
Use a random or building-wide follow-up sampling strategy.
Review crew-assignment and hardware-lot data before inferring a localized source.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant interpreted a small spatial grouping as evidence of a problematic crew or hardware batch concentrated on those floors.
decision_points.time_pressure: No explicit time-pressure condition is reported.
decision_points.uncertainty: The participant retrospectively recognizes that the apparent cluster seemed more diagnostic than it actually was.

decision_points.summary: Grant temporary early occupancy before full alarm and smoke-system integration testing.
evidence_before: The developer faced a financing deadline.
Full alarm and smoke-system integration testing was still approximately three weeks away.
The contractor had a good record on other city projects handled by the participant.
A colleague cited a nearby building that received early partial occupancy and worked out fine.
Departmental five-year data indicated that about 15 percent of atrium smoke-control integration tests required rework.
evidence_after: The trash-chute fire occurred after the temporary-occupancy decision.
The participant said they would probably make the same occupancy decision without new information.
goals_constraints: Balance safety readiness against project financing needs.
Decide whether incomplete integration testing precluded temporary occupancy.
Apply an occupancy threshold under uncertainty.
alternatives: Grant temporary occupancy before integration testing.
Deny or defer occupancy pending full integration testing.
Grant a narrower, condition-limited authorization if permitted by the governing process.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant gave meaningful weight to the contractor's favorable general history and a nearby anecdotal success while treating the citywide rework rate as background rather than decision-driving evidence.
decision_points.time_pressure: High because the developer had a financing deadline while critical integration testing remained incomplete.
decision_points.uncertainty: Material because project-specific integrated smoke-system performance had not yet been verified.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Honestly, the firm's name carried a lot of it. ... I leaned on the fact that this firm doesn't submit sloppy work. If it had been a firm I didn't recognize, I probably would have pushed harder on the input assumptions myself.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision Point 1, participant explanation of the evidence that carried the most weight in approving the CFD-based alternative.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant reduces the level of independent technical scrutiny because the firm is recognized, experienced, and previously approved elsewhere. Credentials and institutional reputation operate as substitutes for the verification that would have been applied to an unfamiliar firm.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: A firm's relevant record and a peer jurisdiction's prior approval are legitimate evidence and may rationally affect review depth under constrained resources. The occurrence is supported because the participant expressly says firm recognition changed the rigor of their assumption-level review.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None for minimum support. A narrowly specified unreviewed CFD input would further strengthen the distinction between calibrated reliance on expertise and excessive deference, but is not necessary.

revision.location: Decision Point 1, the participant's explanation of approval rationale and response concerning outside peer review.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The decision act, authority-related evidence, reduced independent verification, and relevant constraints are all present.
preserve: The participant's contrast between treatment of a recognized and unrecognized firm.
avoid_creating: Do not add a second reputation-based decision at another decision point.
Do not make the participant state that reputation always replaces technical review.
Do not remove the legitimate evidentiary value of firm experience, because that would make the scenario implausible.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “It's hard not to think the smoke migration issue should have jumped out at someone reading that CFD report closely. There was a sensitivity assumption buried in there about stack effect under partial door-open conditions, and looking at it now, it feels like it was sitting right there in the numbers the whole time. At the time, though, it just didn't register as something that mattered.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Post-incident retrospective probe concerning the original design approval, after the trash-chute fire.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: After learning that the atrium did not behave as modeled, the participant retrospectively treats a previously non-salient sensitivity assumption as something that should have been recognized as meaningful from the original report. The later outcome supplies the interpretive significance that was not assigned to the assumption at the time.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Post-incident learning can legitimately identify a previously underappreciated model sensitivity. The occurrence remains supported because the participant does more than learn from the incident: they express a retrospective claim that the issue should have 'jumped out,' despite acknowledging that it did not register as materially diagnostic ex ante.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None for minimum support. The current wording appropriately preserves the subtle distinction between outcome-informed retrospective salience and a claim that the participant knowingly disregarded an obvious warning.

revision.location: Decision Point 1, post-incident reflection beginning “It's hard not to think the smoke migration issue should have jumped out...”
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The episode is temporally distinct from the approval act, identifies a specific original-data element, and demonstrates retrospective elevation of its apparent foreseeability after learning the outcome.
preserve: The post-incident timing of the reflection.
The sensitivity assumption concerning stack effect under partial door-open conditions.
The participant's statement that the assumption did not register as important at the original decision time.
The separation from the authority-bias reasoning used in the original approval.
avoid_creating: Do not add language that the assumption was objectively unmistakable or clearly violated an established requirement.
Do not state that the participant knowingly ignored the assumption at Decision Point 1.
Do not reintroduce a categorical statement that no relevant detail existed in the report, which would undermine the present hindsight mechanism.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Option A might have been the better technical fit, the guidance basically said so, but I didn't want to be defending a judgment call on ‘partially qualitative’ thresholds if something went sideways. B gave me a clean line.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision Point 2, participant explanation for choosing the prescriptive commissioning protocol.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant chooses the option with clear, binary, familiar criteria over an option that is better matched to actual risk conditions but includes less-defined qualitative thresholds.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Clear decision criteria may be justified in public administration because they aid consistency, transparency, auditability, and defensibility. The occurrence is supported because the participant explicitly acknowledges superior technical fit for the more ambiguous option yet rejects it principally to avoid qualitative judgment and accountability exposure.

revision.current_defect: No material defect. The competing options, different threshold clarity, relative technical fit, and participant's weighting are explicit.
preserve: Option B's lower sensitivity to relevant failure modes.
The participant's stated concern about defending qualitative judgment.
avoid_creating: Do not turn the decision into pure schedule pressure or mandatory policy compliance.
Do not add precise probabilities that would change the ambiguity-based mechanism into a numerical risk-calibration problem.
Do not add another preference for familiar procedures elsewhere in the interview.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Out of the whole building, those three stood out to me, and my read was that we had a problem crew or a bad batch of hardware concentrated there.” ... “Crews rotated randomly across the building, actually. And it was three deficiencies out of about 150 doors we'd checked at that point, which is close to what you'd expect ... from ordinary variation. But when you see three flagged floors, it's hard not to read that as meaning something.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision Point 3, interpretation of the three fire-door deficiencies and follow-up question about random crew rotation and sample size.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant infers a localized, systemic crew-level or hardware-level explanation from a small apparent spatial pattern even after identifying that crew assignments were random and the observed count was compatible with ordinary variation.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Reinspecting floors where defects were already found can be a sensible triage action. The biased element is not the targeted follow-up itself; it is the unsupported causal interpretation that the distribution indicates a concentrated crew or hardware problem.

revision.location: Decision Point 3, participant response concerning floors 8, 11, and 14 and the later probe on crew assignment.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The small sample, random allocation context, ordinary-variation comparison, pattern inference, and resulting allocation of inspection effort are all observable.
preserve: The participant's inference of a localized source.
avoid_creating: Do not add floor-specific crew assignment evidence.
Do not add a confirmed hardware-lot defect.
Do not reuse the inspection pattern as a reason for the temporary-occupancy decision.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “This contractor has a good record on other city jobs I've handled, so I felt reasonably confident things would come together.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision Point 4, participant explanation for granting temporary occupancy before full integration testing.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant forecasts a favorable project-specific outcome—successful completion and integration of the atrium alarm and smoke systems—from the contractor's generally favorable performance on other city projects, even though project-specific integration testing remains incomplete.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: A contractor's historical performance is relevant predictive evidence. The occurrence is supported because the cited history is general rather than specific to the unresolved system integration, and the participant's confidence applies to a future project-specific performance question not yet directly tested.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None for minimum support. The distinction between general contractor performance and untested project-specific integration is sufficiently clear.

revision.location: Decision Point 4, participant's first explanation for granting early temporary occupancy.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The future-oriented confidence, general favorable evidence source, and absence of completed project-specific testing are present.
preserve: The contractor's generally good city-project record.
The three-week gap before complete integration testing.
The separate nearby-building anecdote and citywide rework statistic for the probability-neglect occurrence.
avoid_creating: Do not add completed, comparable project-specific functional testing that would fully justify the confidence.
Do not merge contractor history with the nearby-building anecdote.
Do not make the confidence absolute or implausibly reckless.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “A colleague also mentioned a similar building nearby that had gotten early partial occupancy and it worked out fine. I did know our own five-year numbers show something like 15 percent of these atrium smoke-control integration tests need rework citywide, but that felt like a background statistic rather than something specific to this job.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision Point 4, participant explanation of the evidentiary basis for temporary occupancy.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant gives decision weight to a concrete, favorable anecdote while explicitly discounting a relevant available statistical base rate showing that atrium smoke-control integration tests require rework at a non-trivial citywide rate.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The department-wide rework rate may not perfectly transfer to this contractor, building, or design, and the nearby project could have meaningful contextual similarity. The occurrence remains supported because the participant does not identify any specific comparability analysis that would justify treating the anecdote as more decision-relevant than the statistical reference class.

revision.location: Decision Point 4, discussion of the nearby early-occupancy example and the five-year departmental rework data.
revision.current_defect: No material defect. The text provides the statistical base rate, a salient favorable anecdote, and the participant's explicit weighting asymmetry.
preserve: The approximately 15 percent citywide rework rate.
The distinction between statistical evidence and the contractor-reputation rationale.
avoid_creating: Do not replace the anecdote with a statistically representative comparison set.
Do not make the citywide rework statistic project-specific.
Do not add a second base-rate-neglect episode at another decision point.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “A colleague also mentioned a similar building nearby that had gotten early partial occupancy and it worked out fine.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: A vivid, concrete, and easily retrievable local success may receive disproportionate influence relative to aggregate statistical evidence.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The nearby building may have been genuinely comparable in geometry, contractor, permitting conditions, or occupancy safeguards, but no such comparability is established. This evidence is already appropriately captured by the intended base-rate-neglect instance and should not be counted as a separate occurrence.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “Looking at it now, it feels like it was sitting right there in the numbers the whole time.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The later smoke-migration outcome could influence retrospective evaluation of the quality of the original approval decision.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The later incident may legitimately reveal the practical importance of a previously underweighted sensitivity assumption. The text more directly supports hindsight bias because the participant's language concerns retrospective foreseeability rather than a categorical judgment that the decision was bad solely because of the outcome.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “Option B was the old prescriptive smoke test—clear binary pass or fail, easy to defend if anyone questioned it later.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: Selecting an older established process rather than a newer one can superficially resemble a status-quo preference.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The stated operative mechanism is aversion to less-defined qualitative thresholds and concern about accountability, not inertia, switching costs, or preference for a default merely because it is established.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant operated under a statutory 30-day review clock, staffing shortage, lack of peer-review budget, and city pressure to advance housing projects.
nonbias_cues.location: Opening objective discussion and Decision Point 1 context.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: These are organizational constraints that affect available review options. Constraints can coexist with bias but do not independently establish a cognitive-bias mechanism.

nonbias_cues.cue: The firm had extensive relevant experience and a similar design had been approved by a neighboring jurisdiction.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Relevant specialist experience and comparable regulatory precedent can rationally affect confidence. Authority bias arises here only because the participant explicitly lowers independent technical scrutiny because of that status.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant preferred binary commissioning criteria that were easier to defend.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: A regulator may legitimately value consistency, auditability, and explainable thresholds. The ambiguity-effect classification depends on the documented trade-off: the participant recognizes that the less-defined option is better matched to the actual technical risk.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant focused additional inspections on floors where deficiencies were found.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Prioritizing known-deficient locations can be rational inspection triage. The bias concerns the stronger causal inference of a localized systematic source from an insufficient sample.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant reports that the door pattern felt more certain than it probably was in hindsight.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is reflective uncertainty calibration rather than a separate bias occurrence. It describes the participant's recognition of the weakness of the prior inference.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant would probably make the same occupancy decision again without new information.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Maintaining an ex ante judgment after a later incident may reflect appropriate resistance to outcome-driven revision. It does not itself demonstrate overconfidence, hindsight bias, or a poor safety decision.

causal_claims.claim: The engineering firm's reputation and neighboring-jurisdiction approval caused the participant to conduct less independent scrutiny of CFD assumptions.
causal_claims.support: The participant states that the firm's name carried substantial weight and that an unknown firm would have received more assumption-level scrutiny.
causal_claims.assessment: Moderately strong within-person causal attribution. Constraints such as the review clock and lack of peer-review budget are additional contributing conditions, but the participant identifies the reputation-dependent change in review behavior.

causal_claims.claim: Qualitative and less-defined criteria caused rejection of the technically better-matched commissioning protocol.
causal_claims.support: The participant explicitly says they chose Option B because they did not want to defend a judgment call under qualitative thresholds.
causal_claims.assessment: Strong. The alternatives, comparative technical fit, criterion ambiguity, and choice rationale are clearly specified.

causal_claims.claim: The observed door deficiencies were caused by a localized problem crew or hardware batch.
causal_claims.support: The participant makes this inference from three flagged floors.
causal_claims.assessment: Weak. Random crew rotation and a small count compatible with ordinary variation undercut the inference that the spatial pattern establishes a localized cause.

causal_claims.claim: The contractor's favorable general history and a nearby successful early-occupancy example supported confidence that this building's incomplete integration testing would resolve successfully.
causal_claims.support: The participant invokes both sources when explaining the temporary-occupancy decision.
causal_claims.assessment: Weak to moderate. The evidence may have predictive relevance, but the interview provides no demonstration that the prior jobs or nearby building were materially comparable to the untested atrium smoke-system integration conditions.

causal_claims.claim: The later smoke-migration experience showed that a sensitivity assumption in the original CFD report should have been recognized as important during the original approval.
causal_claims.support: The participant says the issue should have jumped out and retrospectively experiences the assumption as having been present in the numbers all along, while admitting it did not register as significant before the incident.
causal_claims.assessment: Epistemically weak as an ex ante foreseeability claim but coherent as a hindsight-bias mechanism. The incident can reveal the importance of an assumption without proving that its significance was clear at the original decision point.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: A three-floor distribution of deficiencies is interpreted as evidence of a crew-specific or hardware-batch-specific cause.
correlation_causation_risks.why_risky: The sample is small, crews rotated randomly, and the observed rate is described as compatible with ordinary variation. The pattern does not establish causal concentration.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: General contractor success and one nearby building's successful early occupancy are treated as evidence of readiness for this particular untested integrated smoke-control system.
correlation_causation_risks.why_risky: The interview does not establish comparability of design, subcontractors, commissioning readiness, system configuration, occupancy safeguards, or project-specific defects.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: The subsequent trash-chute fire is used to treat the previously non-salient CFD sensitivity assumption as retrospectively foreseeable.
correlation_causation_risks.why_risky: The outcome changes the salience and interpretation of the earlier data. It does not independently demonstrate that a reviewer should have assigned the same significance to the assumption before the outcome occurred.

causal_audit.explanation: The interview presents a coherent four-decision chronology and keeps the principal evidence sources reasonably distinct across occurrences. Decision Point 1 contains two separable reasoning operations: initial reputation-based evidence weighting and later post-incident retrospective attribution. Decision Point 4 also separates general contractor-history optimism from anecdote-versus-base-rate weighting. No paired counterfactual is present in the interview itself; the hidden specification's engineering-firm-reputation counterfactual variable is a generation design element rather than an executed interview condition.

global_revision_constraints: Keep authority bias tied to the original approval act and hindsight bias tied to the post-incident reflection.
Keep contractor-history optimism distinct from the anecdotal-success versus citywide-base-rate comparison.
Do not add explicit bias labels or didactic explanations.
Do not alter the stated engineering-firm-reputation counterfactual variable or introduce additional causal changes if the interview is later adapted into a paired counterfactual condition.
Treat the availability and outcome-bias cues as overlapping candidates, not as additional countable target occurrences.
